claim: Nearly 100 million adults in the United States are prescribed a benzodiazepine annually.
source: An estimated nearly 100 million adults in the United States are prescribed a BZD annually (Agarwal and Landon, 2019; Bachhuber et al., 2016; Olfson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Agarwal and Landon, 2019; Bachhuber et al., 2016; Olfson et al., 2015).

claim: Benzodiazepines have anxiolytic and sedative properties used as therapies for conditions including anxiety, panic, insomnia, seizures, muscle spasms, pain, and alcohol withdrawal.
source: Their anxiolytic and sedative properties are used as therapies for conditions including anxiety, panic, insomnia, seizures, muscle spasms, pain, and alcohol withdrawal (Möhler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Möhler et al., 2002).

claim: Benzodiazepines have undesirable effects including tolerance, addiction, dependence, and withdrawal symptoms.
source: Although largely effective, BZDs have undesirable effects, including tolerance, addiction, dependence, and withdrawal symptoms, and are often co-abused with alcohol and opioids (Fluyau et al., 2018; Schmitz, 2016; Jones and McAninch, 2015; Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fluyau et al., 2018; Schmitz, 2016; Jones and McAninch, 2015; Jones et al., 2010).

claim: Benzodiazepines are often co-abused with alcohol and opioids.
source: Although largely effective, BZDs have undesirable effects, including tolerance, addiction, dependence, and withdrawal symptoms, and are often co-abused with alcohol and opioids (Fluyau et al., 2018; Schmitz, 2016; Jones and McAninch, 2015; Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fluyau et al., 2018; Schmitz, 2016; Jones and McAninch, 2015; Jones et al., 2010).

claim: The therapeutic effects of benzodiazepines are conferred upon binding to and modulating the activity of GABAA receptors.
source: The therapeutic effects of BZDs are conferred upon binding to and modulating the activity of GABAARs, which are the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter-gated ion channels in the central nervous system (Smart and Stephenson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Smart and Stephenson, 2019).

claim: GABAA receptors are the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter-gated ion channels in the central nervous system.
source: The therapeutic effects of BZDs are conferred upon binding to and modulating the activity of GABAARs, which are the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter-gated ion channels in the central nervous system (Smart and Stephenson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Smart and Stephenson, 2019).

claim: GABAA receptors are part of the Cys-loop superfamily of pentameric ligand-gated ion channels.
source: GABAARs are part of the Cys-loop superfamily of pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) including homologous glycine (Gly), nicotinic acetylcholine (nACh), serotonin type 3 (5-HT3), and zinc-activated receptors as well as prokaryotic homologs (Pless and Sivilotti, 2018; Nemecz et al., 2016; Tasneem et al., 2004; Connolly and Wafford, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Pless and Sivilotti, 2018; Nemecz et al., 2016; Tasneem et al., 2004; Connolly and Wafford, 2004).

claim: Each pentameric GABAA receptor is comprised of subtype-specific combinations of five homologous but nonidentical subunits that together form a central chloride conducting pore.
source: Each pentameric GABAAR is comprised of subtype-specific combinations of five homologous but nonidentical subunits (α1-6, β1-3, γ1-3, δ, ε, π, θ, ρ1-3) that together form a central chloride conducting pore (Figure 1; Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Olsen and Sieghart, 2008) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The most prominent GABAA receptor subtype at synapses is comprised of α1, βn, and γ2 subunits.
source: The most prominent subtype at synapses is comprised of α1, βn, and γ2 subunits (Sieghart and Sperk, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Sieghart and Sperk, 2002).

claim: GABAA receptor dysfunction is related to disorders such as epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, schizophrenia, and neurodevelopmental disorders such as fragile X syndrome.
source: GABAARs provide a critical balance with excitatory signaling for normal neural function, and not surprisingly, their dysfunction is related to disorders such as epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, schizophrenia, and neurodevelopmental disorders such as fragile X syndrome (Hernandez and Macdonald, 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Mahdavi et al., 2018; Braat and Kooy, 2015; Vien et al., 2015; Rudolph and Möhler, 2014; Limon et al., 2012; Ramamoorthi and Lin, 2011; Solís-Añez et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hernandez and Macdonald, 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Mahdavi et al., 2018; Braat and Kooy, 2015; Vien et al., 2015; Rudolph and Möhler, 2014; Limon et al., 2012; Ramamoorthi and Lin, 2011; Solís-Añez et al., 2007).

claim: Recent cryo-EM models of heteromeric GABAA receptors with bound neurotransmitter and benzodiazepine show that benzodiazepines are bound at a specific recognition site in the extracellular domain between α and γ subunits.
source: In conjunction with structural models of mostly homomeric pLGICs, recent cryo-EM models of heteromeric GABAARs with bound neurotransmitter and BZD provide an important conceptual aid to understand the mechanism of action of these drugs (Kim et al., 2020; Masiulis et al., 2019; Laverty et al., 2019; Phulera et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018). Consistent with earlier functional studies (Sigel and Ernst, 2018; Sigel and Lüscher, 2011; Sigel, 2002; Wagner and Czajkowski, 2001; Kucken et al., 2000; McKernan et al., 1998; Pritchett et al., 1989; Gibbs et al., 1985), they show that BZDs are bound at a specific recognition site in the extracellular domain between α and γ subunits (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2020; Masiulis et al., 2019; Laverty et al., 2019; Phulera et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018; Sigel and Ernst, 2018; Sigel and Lüscher, 2011; Sigel, 2002; Wagner and Czajkowski, 2001; Kucken et al., 2000; McKernan et al., 1998; Pritchett et al., 1989; Gibbs et al., 1985) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Benzodiazepines do not evoke robust channel opening by themselves, but instead modulate responses to an agonist such as GABA.
source: However, these approaches are challenged for BZDs because they do not evoke robust channel opening by themselves, but instead modulate responses to an agonist such as GABA.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about BZD function.

claim: The ability of benzodiazepides to potentiate current responses to saturating concentrations of partial agonists, and also to directly gate gain of function mutants, implies that the drug's effect is not due to changes in binding alone.
source: The ability of BZDs to potentiate current responses to saturating concentrations of partial agonists, and also to directly gate gain of function mutants, implies that the drug's effect is not due to changes in binding alone.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: The gain of function mutant α1L9'Tβ2γ2L is spontaneously active and directly gated by benzodiazepines alone.
source: Here we examined linkage between the BZD site and pore gate in isolation from any effect of the drug on agonist binding using a spontaneously active gain of function mutant (α1L9'Tβ2γ2L) that is directly gated by BZDs alone (Scheller and Forman, 2002; Chang and Weiss, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Scheller and Forman, 2002; Chang and Weiss, 1999).

claim: The M2–M3 linker is a loop following the pore lining M2 helix that together with several other important interfacial loops defines the region connecting extracellular ligand binding and transmembrane domains known to be crucially involved in the gating process of pentameric ligand-gated ion channels.
source: The M2–M3 linker is a loop following the pore lining M2 helix that together with several other important interfacial loops defines the region connecting extracellular ligand binding and transmembrane domains known to be crucially involved in the gating process of pLGICs (Figure 1).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Structural models show that agonist binding is associated with an outward displacement of the M2–M3 linker from the central pore axis.
source: Structural models show that agonist binding is associated with an outward displacement of the M2–M3 linker from the central pore axis (Nemecz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nemecz et al., 2016).

claim: Mutations in the M2–M3 linker generally impair gating by agonists.
source: Mutations in the linker generally impair gating by agonists (Kash et al., 2003; O'Shea and Harrison, 2000), and some are associated with genetic diseases such as epilepsy in GABAARs (Hales et al., 2006; Hernandez and Macdonald, 2019) or hyperekplexia in GlyRs (Bode and Lynch, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kash et al., 2003; O'Shea and Harrison, 2000).

claim: Some M2–M3 linker mutations are associated with genetic diseases such as epilepsy in GABAA receptors or hyperekplexia in glycine receptors.
source: Mutations in the linker generally impair gating by agonists (Kash et al., 2003; O'Shea and Harrison, 2000), and some are associated with genetic diseases such as epilepsy in GABAARs (Hales et al., 2006; Hernandez and Macdonald, 2019) or hyperekplexia in GlyRs (Bode and Lynch, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hales et al., 2006; Hernandez and Macdonald, 2019; Bode and Lynch, 2014).

claim: Alanine substitutions throughout the α1M2–M3 linker generally impair unliganded pore gating.
source: We show that alanine substitutions throughout the α1M2–M3 linker generally impair unliganded pore gating, whereas they have little effect on the efficiency by which chemical energy from DZ binding is transmitted to the pore gate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2, 3).

claim: Alanine substitutions throughout the α1M2–M3 linker have little effect on the efficiency by which chemical energy from diazepam binding is transmitted to the pore gate.
source: We show that alanine substitutions throughout the α1M2–M3 linker generally impair unliganded pore gating, whereas they have little effect on the efficiency by which chemical energy from DZ binding is transmitted to the pore gate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 4, 5, 7).

claim: All alanine mutations in the α1M2–M3 linker exhibited an increase in the EC50 and/or steepness of the GABA concentration–response relationship compared to α1L9'T.
source: As compared to α1L9'T, all of the alanine mutations exhibited an increase in the EC50 and/or steepness of the GABA concentration–response relationship (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increased EC50 for GABA in α1M2–M3 linker mutations is generally consistent with previous reports in a wild-type background.
source: The increased EC50 is generally consistent with previous reports of α1M2–M3 linker mutations in a wild-type background (O'Shea and Harrison, 2000) and implies that side chain interactions in this region are important for channel gating by agonists.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (O'Shea and Harrison, 2000).

claim: Side chain interactions in the α1M2–M3 linker region are important for channel gating by agonists.
source: The increased EC50 is generally consistent with previous reports of α1M2–M3 linker mutations in a wild-type background (O'Shea and Harrison, 2000) and implies that side chain interactions in this region are important for channel gating by agonists.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations and prior literature.

claim: All α1M2–M3 linker mutations except for α1P277A reduced the unliganded open probability by approximately two-fold.
source: Under the assumption that Po-GABA-max is similar for all constructs, all α1M2–M3 linker mutations except for α1P277A reduced the unliganded open probability by approximately two-fold (Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The open probability in saturating GABA (Po-GABA-max) is approximately 0.85 in wild-type channels.
source: Po-GABA-max is ~0.85 in wild-type channels (Keramidas and Harrison, 2010), and likely to be closer to 1.0 in a gain of function background such as α1L9'T that is further known to desensitize much more slowly than wild-type (Scheller and Forman, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Keramidas and Harrison, 2010; Scheller and Forman, 2002).

claim: Alanine substitutions in the α1M2–M3 linker have no obvious effect on diazepam concentration–response relationships with the exception of α1L276A that confers a right shift and reduction in steepness.
source: Alanine substitutions in the α1M2–M3 linker have no obvious effect on DZ concentration–response relationships with the exception of α1L276A that confers a right shift and reduction in steepness (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reports for the EC50 of diazepam potentiation in wild-type receptors are similar to the diazepam EC50 for α1L9'T receptors.
source: Reports for the EC50 of DZ potentiation in wild-type receptors are similar to the DZ EC50 for α1L9'T receptors reported here and in previous studies (Li et al., 2013; Campo-Soria et al., 2006; Rüsch and Forman, 2005; Walters et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2013; Campo-Soria et al., 2006; Rüsch and Forman, 2005; Walters et al., 2000).

claim: The ratio of maximal diazepam-evoked current amplitude to PTX-sensitive current amplitude is largely independent of alanine substitution in the α1M2–M3 linker with the notable exception of α1V279A.
source: The ratio of the maximal DZ-evoked current amplitude (IDZ-max) to PTX-sensitive current amplitude (IPTX) is a measure for how well DZ activates the channel relative to its spontaneous unliganded activity. This ratio is largely independent of alanine substitution in the α1M2–M3 linker with the notable exception of α1V279A (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: α1V279 has a unique role in diazepam modulation, whereas side chains of other linker residues are involved little or not at all.
source: This suggests that α1V279 has a unique role in DZ modulation, whereas side chains of other linker residues are involved little or not at all.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: The valine at position 279 in the GABAA receptor α1 subunit is located near the center of the M2–M3 linker and is nearly always an aliphatic residue in different GABAA receptor subunits as well as in subunits of other pentameric ligand-gated ion channels.
source: The valine at position 279 in the GABAAR α1 subunit is located near the center of the linker and is nearly always an aliphatic residue in different GABAAR subunits as well as in subunits of other pLGICs, with the exception of AChR, where it is a threonine.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and structural knowledge.

claim: The mutation α1V279D severely inhibits unliganded gating, exhibiting very little PTX-sensitive current in relation to robust currents evoked with saturating GABA.
source: The negative charge introduced by α1V279D severely inhibits unliganded gating, exhibiting very little PTX-sensitive current in relation to robust currents evoked with saturating GABA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claim: The mutation α1V279W only slightly impairs unliganded gating to a similar degree as substitution with alanine.
source: In contrast, addition of the bulky side chain α1V279W only slightly impairs unliganded gating to a similar degree as substitution with alanine.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claim: Side chain volume at position 279 is less critical for unliganded gating, whereas introduction of a negative charge nearly abolishes spontaneous activity despite the α1L9'T pore mutation.
source: These data suggest that side chain volume at this position is less critical for unliganded gating, whereas introduction of a negative charge nearly abolishes spontaneous activity despite the α1L9'T pore mutation.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: The mutation α1V279D increases the GABA EC50 by approximately 100-fold.
source: Consistent with impaired pore gating, α1V279D increases the GABA EC50 by ~100-fold.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claim: The ratio of diazepam-evoked to PTX-sensitive current amplitude is only slightly increased by α1V279W.
source: The ratio of DZ-evoked to PTX-sensitive current amplitude is only slightly increased by α1V279W, whereas it is further increased by α1V279D, albeit not to the extent of α1V279A (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Diazepam gating is specifically enhanced by a reduction of side chain volume at position 279.
source: These data suggest that DZ gating is specifically enhanced by a reduction of side chain volume at position 279.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: Diazepam binding confers a uniform ΔΔGDZ = ΔG1− ΔG0 = −0.4 kcal/mol to the pore gating equilibrium independent of α1M2–M3 linker mutation with the notable exception of α1V279A that more than doubles ΔΔGDZ.
source: A comparison of ΔG0 versus ΔG1 shows that DZ binding confers a uniform ΔΔGDZ = ΔG1− ΔG0 = −0.4 kcal/mol to the pore gating equilibrium independent of α1M2–M3 linker mutation with the notable exception f α1V279A that more than doubles ΔΔGDZ (Figure 7B,C and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, 7C and Table 1.

claim: Coupling between the benzodiazepine site and pore gate is relatively independent of individual α1M2–M3 linker side chain interactions except for α1V279, which natively hinders diazepam gating as compared to its substitution with alanine.
source: These observations suggest that coupling between the BZD site and pore gate is relatively independent of individual α1M2–M3 linker side chain interactions except for α1V279, which natively hinders DZ gating as compared to its substitution with alanine.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: Introduction of a bulky tryptophan or charged aspartate at position 279 have much smaller effects on ΔΔGDZ than alanine substitution.
source: Strikingly, introduction of a bulky tryptophan or charged aspartate at position 279 have much smaller effects on ΔΔGDZ, consistent with the idea that the small side chain volume of alanine is the most relevant factor for increased DZ efficiency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 7).

claim: GABA EC50 is increased by α1V279A in a wild-type background.
source: First, GABA EC50 is increased by α1V279A, consistent with impaired unliganded gating (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Diazepam potentiates GABA-evoked peak current responses to a greater extent in V279A than in wild-type receptors.
source: Second, DZ potentiates GABA-evoked peak current responses to a greater extent in V279A than in wild-type receptors, consistent with enhanced coupling between the BZD site and pore gate in the mutant (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: Diazepam potentiates V279A currents evoked with a saturating concentration of GABA.
source: In contrast to wild-type, DZ also potentiates V279A currents evoked with a saturating concentration of GABA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 8).

claim: The additional diazepam modulation conferred by α1V279A is both independent of agonist association and additive to diazepam potentiation in wild-type receptors.
source: Together, these data suggest that the additional DZ modulation conferred by α1V279A is both independent of agonist association and additive to DZ potentiation in wild-type receptors.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations.

claim: Responses to approximately EC20-25 GABA were reduced in the presence of FG-7142 in both wild-type and V279A receptors, but to a slightly lesser extent in V279A.
source: Responses to ~EC20-25 GABA were reduced in the presence of FG-7142 in both WT and V279A receptors, but to a slightly lesser extent in V279A (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: α1L9'T and α1V279A have independent and additive effects on the pore-gating equilibrium.
source: These results suggest that α1L9'T and α1V279A have independent and additive effects on the gating equilibrium, and that for α1V279A, this effect depends on DZ occupancy.
evidence: Based on logical inference from model simulations and experimental observations.

claim: The model's predicted maximum open probability approached 1.0 in the α1L9'T background, consistent with a gain of function phenotype.
source: The model's predicted maximum Po approached 1.0 in the α1L9'T background, consistent with a gain of function phenotype.
evidence: Based on model simulations and inference.

claim: Maximal open probability was reduced in α1V279Aβ2γ2L as compared to wild-type receptors.
source: In contrast, maximal Po was reduced in α1V279Aβ2γ2L as compared to wild-type receptors, as expected for a reduction in unliganded activity.
evidence: Based on model simulations and inference.

claim: Estimates for the energetic effect of diazepam binding on pore gating (−0.4 kcal/mol) are similar to prior estimates from direct gating in L9'S/T backgrounds and from kinetic models.
source: Our estimates for the energetic effect of DZ binding on pore gating (−0.4 kcal/mol) are similar to prior estimates from direct gating in L9'S/T backgrounds and from kinetic models (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2014; Gielen et al., 2012; Downing et al., 2005; Rüsch and Forman, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2014; Gielen et al., 2012; Downing et al., 2005; Rüsch and Forman, 2005).

claim: The energetic effect of diazepam binding on pore gating is approximately 10-fold less than the energy derived from binding each molecule of GABA.
source: This is approximately 10-fold less than the energy derived from binding each molecule of GABA (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2014; Maksay, 1994; Jackson, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2014; Maksay, 1994; Jackson, 1992).

claim: The M2–M3 linker is associated with early movements during acetylcholine receptor activation.
source: Given that the M2–M3 linker is associated with early movements during AChR activation (Purohit et al., 2013), it is possible that biasing the linker toward its active conformation in the α1L9'T background could limit our ability to observe its full range of motion.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Purohit et al., 2013).

claim: The interface between the extracellular agonist- and benzodiazepine-binding domains and the transmembrane helices is formed largely by several loops including the M2–M3 linker, Cys loop, β1–β2 loop and β8–β9 linker, and pre-M1 segment from neighboring subunits.
source: The interface between the extracellular agonist- and BZD-binding domains and the transmembrane helices is formed largely by several loops including the M2–M3 linker, Cys loop, β1–β2 loop and β8–β9 linker, and pre-M1 segment from neighboring subunits (Figure 1).
evidence: Draws from established structural knowledge and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Mutagenesis suggests that interactions between extracellular and transmembrane domains are important for channel gating by agonists.
source: Mutagenesis suggests that interactions between these domains are important for channel gating by agonists (Kash et al., 2003; O'Shea and Harrison, 2000) thought to involve an outward radial displacement of the M2–M3 linker (Nemecz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kash et al., 2003; O'Shea and Harrison, 2000; Nemecz et al., 2016).

claim: Rate versus free energy linear relationships in acetylcholine receptor suggest that the M2–M3 linker moves early during channel activation, similar to rearrangements at agonist binding sites.
source: Rate versus free energy linear relationships in AChR suggest that the M2–M3 linker moves early during channel activation, similar to rearrangements at agonist binding sites (Purohit et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Purohit et al., 2013).

claim: Mutant cycle analysis indicates strong long-range coupling between residues in the M2–M3 linker and agonist binding sites.
source: Consistent with these observations, mutant cycle analysis indicates strong long-range coupling between residues in the M2–M3 linker and agonist binding sites (Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gupta et al., 2017).

claim: In structural models, the M2–M3 linker adopts a C-shaped conformation with α1V279 oriented inwards toward the center of the arc.
source: In structural models, the M2–M3 linker adopts a C-shaped conformation with α1V279 oriented inwards toward the center of the arc (Figure 1D; Kim et al., 2020; Laverty et al., 2019; Masiulis et al., 2019; Phulera et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2020; Laverty et al., 2019; Masiulis et al., 2019; Phulera et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2018) and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The side chain at position 279 is centrally involved in steric interactions between linker residues near the top of the M2 and M3 helices.
source: We hypothesize that the side chain at position 279 is centrally involved in steric interactions between linker residues near the top of the M2 and M3 helices.
evidence: Involves hypothetical reasoning based on structural and functional data.

claim: Removing the obstruction at position 279 (α1V279A) would allow the linker to become more compact and bring the M2 and M3 helices closer together.
source: Removing this obstruction (α1V279A) would allow the linker to become more compact and bring the M2 and M3 helices closer together.
evidence: Involves hypothetical reasoning based on structural considerations.

claim: A more compact transmembrane domain may enhance coupling with the benzodiazepine site.
source: Conversely, a more compact transmembrane domain may also enhance coupling with the BZD site (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: Involves speculative reasoning supported by citation to published literature (Kim et al., 2020).

claim: Valine and threonine residues in glycine receptor and acetylcholine receptor aligning with V279 adopt a similar conformation.
source: Valine and threonine residues in GlyR and AchR aligning with V279 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) adopt a similar conformation (Kumar et al., 2020; Nemecz et al., 2016; Du et al., 2015), suggesting that this residue has a conserved role in other pLGICs.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kumar et al., 2020; Nemecz et al., 2016; Du et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The β8-β9 linker and pre-M1 in the neighboring γ2 subunit come in close proximity to the α1M2–M3 linker and are known to be important for benzodiazepine modulation.
source: The β8-β9 linker and pre-M1 in the neighboring γ2 subunit come in close proximity to the α1M2–M3 linker and are known to be important for BZD modulation, with the β8-β9 linker also contributing to the BZD-binding site (Hanson and Czajkowski, 2011; Hanson and Czajkowski, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hanson and Czajkowski, 2011; Hanson and Czajkowski, 2008).

claim: In acetylcholine receptor strong coupling with the adjacent β8-β9 linker and pre-M1 segment of the neighboring subunit occurs primarily via the threonine aligning with α1V279 in GABAA receptor and its neighboring serine.
source: In AChR strong coupling with the adjacent β8-β9 linker and pre-M1 segment of the neighboring subunit occurs primarily via the threonine aligning with α1V279 in GABAAR and its neighboring serine (Gupta et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gupta et al., 2017).

claim: Comparison of glycine receptor structures in apo or antagonist-bound versus agonist-bound conformations indicates that intersubunit interactions between the M2–M3 linker in the vicinity of the valine aligning with V279 and the following serine, and the top of the M1 helix in the adjacent subunit are weakened during channel activation.
source: Comparison of GlyR structures in apo or antagonist-bound versus agonist-bound conformations indicates that intersubunit interactions between the M2–M3 linker in the vicinity of the valine aligning with V279 and the following serine, and the top of the M1 helix in the adjacent subunit are weakened during channel activation (Du et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Du et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

claim: Recent structures of αβγ receptors show diazepam bound not only at the classical α/γ site in the extracellular domain, but also in the transmembrane domain below the M2–M3 linker at β/α and γ/β intersubunit interfaces.
source: Recent structures of αβγ receptors show DZ bound not only at the classical α/γ site in the extracellular domain, but also in the transmembrane domain below the M2–M3 linker at β/α and γ/β intersubunit interfaces (Kim et al., 2020; Masiulis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2020; Masiulis et al., 2019).

claim: The relevance of transmembrane diazepam binding sites to high affinity binding of approximately 1 μM diazepam at the classical site is unclear.
source: However, these structures were solved in the presence of 100–200 μM DZ, and the relevance of these transmembrane sites to high affinity binding of ~1 μM DZ at the classical site is unclear (Walters et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on logical inference from structural data and citation to published literature (Walters et al., 2000).

claim: Diazepam binding in the transmembrane domain was not observed at α/γ or α/β interfaces.
source: Also, DZ binding in the transmembrane domain was not observed at α/γ or α/β interfaces.
evidence: Based on structural data from cited literature.

claim: The observed effects of α1V279A reflect altered functional coupling with the classical benzodiazepine site.
source: Therefore, we favor the interpretation that our observed effects reflect altered functional coupling with the classical site.
evidence: Based on logical inference from experimental observations and structural considerations.

claim: The residue V279 in the α1M2–M3 linker regulates energetic coupling between the benzodiazepine site and the pore gate.
source: Our observations reveal a critical residue V279 in the α1M2–M3 linker, which regulates energetic coupling between the BZD site and the pore gate, whereas other linker side chains contribute little or not at all.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.
